messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm working on a project looking a referral network of cancer services
organizations for low-income cancer patients (what predicts organization A
referring a patient to organization B). One of the predictors of referrals
that I am using is a network of distance (in minutes) on public
transportation between the organizations. I am using the dyadcov term in my
ERGM to predict the presence of a referral tie between two organizations
based on how far apart they are. My question is: How would I interpret the
following:

dyadcov.minutes.mutual       -28.44480    0.06961        NA  < 1e-04 ***
dyadcov.minutes.utri         -15.46894    0.11195        NA  < 1e-04 ***
dyadcov.minutes.ltri         -15.42000    0.10858        NA  < 1e-04 ***

The first row appears to be the reduction in likelihood of a tie for a 1
unit increase in minutes between organizations when A refers to B and B
refers to A (there are referral links going both directions).

The upper triangle is then likely to be the reduction in the likelihood of a
tie for a 1 unit increase in minutes when A refers to B (but B does not
refer to A)

The lower triangle is the reduction in the likelihood of a tie for a 1 unit
increase in minutes when B refers to A (but A does not refer to B)

I gather from the statnet tutorials that each dyad only falls into one of
these categories....mutual, upper, or lower

Does this sound like an appropriate interpretation of these results?

Thanks in advance for any thoughts on this.

Jenine

messages.body_plain:
I'm a graduate student trying to figure out Add Health's social
network data and I'm hoping that, because it is widely used, someone
on this list could offer a little guidance.  Also, feel free to inform me
if I'm breaking list protocol in any way.

My primary goal is to predict "popularity."  I figured I'd create and
predict multiple measures of centrality and try to think about how
they differ.  I can read the documentation to learn how to create
those measures in general.  But I'm wondering, -here is my first question-
has anyone written up anything specific to manipulating the Ad Health
network data.


That alone would be enormously helpful, but if you want to comment on
another issue that would be great.  Here it is: popularity cannot be
directly measured, and various facts about the way data is collected
are going to bias any measure of popularity I use.  I face the
following questions: what are the ways I expect various measures of
popularity to be biased and how can I correct for them.

One way to categorize biases in the measures would be those that
affect school/grade-level means and those that affect variation within
schools/grades.  Some of the biases I'm thinking about are school
size, fraction absent or otherwise not providing usable data, and
fraction of friends outside the school. Sometimes students nominate
someone that they say is in the school but does not show up on the
roster which indicates the accuracy of the roster could be an issue.

I see two potentially complementary ways to approach correcting for
these biases.  One is to build the correction into my measure of
centrality.  The other is that when I model these influences when I am
predicting the measure of centrality (with some kind of mixed effects
model).  Right now I'm just working with In-Degree so I'm
experimenting with the latter approach but I'd like to consider the
former now that I'm ready to construct new measures of centrality.

I'm sorry this email got so long.  Please don't feel a burden to solve
my research problems, but if you can point me in the right direction
that would be great.

Many thanks,
Mike

Ph.D. Student
Sociology Department
University of Chicago

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jacob.  Since you didn't provide an example to test, I invented  
one.  This might explain the problem:

 > nw=network.initialize(5)
 > nw[1,2]=nw[3,4]=nw[4,5]=1
 > slfctrl_s <- c(1, 1, 2, 2, NA)
 > nw %v% "slfctrl_s" <- slfctrl_s
 > ergm(nw~nodecov("slfctrl_s"))
Error in ergm.pl(Clist = Clist, Clist.miss = Clist.miss, m = m,  
theta.offset = theta.offset,  :
   NA/NaN/Inf in foreign function call (arg 11)

This (above) appears to be the same error you got.  However, note that  
your fix does not work:

 > slfctrl_s[is.na(slfctrl_s)] <- mean(slfctrl_s, na.rm = TRUE)
 > ergm(nw~nodecov("slfctrl_s"))
Error in ergm.pl(Clist = Clist, Clist.miss = Clist.miss, m = m,  
theta.offset = theta.offset,  :
   NA/NaN/Inf in foreign function call (arg 11)

The reason is that you did not change the vertex attribute in the nw  
object.  The code below does this and fixes the error:

 > nw %v% "slfctrl_s" <- slfctrl_s
 > ergm(nw~nodecov("slfctrl_s"))
Newton-Raphson iterations:  4

MLE Coefficients:
nodecov.slfctrl_s
           -0.5485


Hope this helps!



Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] interpreting GWDSP?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jenine,

I don't know if you got a response to this question, and I just ran 
across something that might help, so thought I'd send it to you.
Danny Wyatt (from here at UW) sent us a short description, and I made up a 
little excel spreadsheet to see if I could get some intuition (attached).

Briefly, these terms (GWESP, GWDSP, and GWDEG) fit a 2 parameter curve to 
the histogram of the number of shared partners, or degree.  The two 
parameters, alpha and w, define the shape of this curve.  The alpha term 
acts a bit like an intercept (in a non-linear way), and the coefficient 
(w) acts a bit like a slope (again, in a non-linear way)

Danny's explanation below.  Hope this helps.

best,
Martina

> Anyhow, have you read this paper by David Hunter?
> Curved exponential family models for social networks, Social Networks
> 29(2). 216-230.
> http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.socnet.2006.08.005
>
> It helped me understand the GW* features a lot better.  In particular
> Eqn. 16 in that papers works it out so that you can interpret your
> parameters as the log odds of a node increasing its degree from k to
> k+1---or for GWESP the log odds that a pair will change their number
> of shared partners from k to k+1.
>
> The general form of that is
> w * (1 - exp(-alpha))^k
> where w is the regular non-alpha parameter.
>
> So if you've fixed alpha=0.2, then it's just w * (0.181)^k.  You could
> plot that out for k from 0 to N-2 (if you've got N people) and it'll
> show you how the log odds of adding a new shared partner decreases as
> you have more shared partners.
>
> Actually, if you exp it to get the odds it'll approach 1 and you can
> find the point where it's close enough to 1 for you and then say "this
> is the point at which its no longer beneficial for two people to keep
> adding mutual friends."

messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I had a question that I am hoping someone here with more experience  
with ERG models might have some input.

Background on Project: I am using ERG models to examine the patters of  
advice networks in traditional settings related to acquiring  
skills/knowledge. I am interested in empirically testing if a variety  
of attributes (perceived skill, age, gender, etc.), suggested by  
analytical modeling to be important, are related to the patterns of  
these networks and the number of nominations that an individual  
receives. The way that the data was collected, we allowed individuals  
to nominate at most 5 other people, which I am including as a  
constraint in all models.

I am unsure whether to include edges as a constraint or as a parameter  
to estimate.  When I include it as a parameter, all my main effects  
parameters (nodeicov) are strongly correlated (above .8) with the  
edges parameter (and with each other). When I constrain the simulated  
networks to match the number of edges present in the observed data, I  
no longer have this problem, but the parameter estimates are different  
(same direction, but different magnitudes).

Theoretically, I think that varying the number of total ties present  
in the network is important, since there are reasons to think that  
this might happen in the real world.  However, the correlation between  
this parameter and all the main effects is troubling.

Does anyone have any thoughts on what is more important, not having  
strong correlations between predictors, or having a model that is  
allowed to vary in ways that are similar to what we might expect in  
reality?

Any input is appreciated,

James Broesch

PhD Candidate
Department of Anthropology
Emory University

messages.body_plain:
Hey everyone,
I have a simple problem that I hope has a simple solution:

I am working on a social network of birds (43 individuals in this network),
each with a unique ID number, ranging from 7 to 112998.

When I import an edge list based on these ID numbers using network(), it
creates a vertex for all numbers up to 112998 (remember, there are actually
only 43 individuals).
I can get around this by assigning the ID numbers as factors, but this then
creates a separate problem: Now, when I create an adjacency matrix, it sorts
them by the first digit, then second digit such that 112998 comes before
256, which comes before 7. However, if I sort a list of vertex attributes
using the same IDs, it sorts them correctly in numerical order. This means
that my attribute list and the vertex list does not match up!

Is there a way to get statnet to recognize my ID names as numbers, but not
create vertices for all possible numbers up to 112998?

Any clues would be greatly appreciated,

Dai Shizuka
----------

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Dai -

The issue here is that the edgelist->network conversion assumes that 
your data is given in the form of vertex IDs (since you are using a 
numeric matrix).  Vertex IDs are not names, but the sort order of the 
vertex; thus, you can't have an ID (in the sense of the network package) 
of 112998 on a 43-node network.  You can, of course, have a vertex that 
carries this number as a name (or other attribute).

As this suggests, one approach is to renumber your edgelists prior to 
conversion.  E.g., something like this:

#Let el be your edgelist matrix
uvert<-sort(unique(c(el[,1],el[,2])))
el[,1]<-match(el[,1],uvert)
el[,2]<-match(el[,2],uvert)

This will keep your network vertex IDs in the same order as your own ID 
numbers (names).  Then, set the vertex names (or any other attribute) 
equal to uvert; you can retrieve the original names in the usual fashion 
using %v% or get.vertex.attribute.

If you don't like that road, another option is to convert your numbers 
to fixed-width character strings with leading zeros.  (formatC will do 
this.)  That ensures that the sort order matches the numeric order of 
your vertex names.  Finally, you could just create the network as usual, 
and then permute the vertices into your desired order using 
permute.vertexIDs (with the order identified by 
order(as.numeric(vertex.names(mynet))) or some such).

Any of these should work, but I recommend the first, FWIW.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I had a number of potential solutions to my problem. There were two
particularly good solutions (by Dr. Carter Butts, no surprisingly)... So I'm
going to post here my problem and the two solutions for anyone who might
encounter this issue in the future. I apologize for the long post.

The problem: unique ID numbers get interpreted by statnet as a continuous
parameter. So, when trying to turn an edge list composed of these ID numbers
into a network object, it will try to create a node for every possible
number from 1 to the largest ID number. This screws up the data. You can get
around this problem by converting ID numbers to character strings, but when
you have ID numbers that are different numbers of digits, then it will sort
them weirdly when constructing the adjacency matrix. I'm going to
demonstrate the problem with two examples, and then provide the two
suggested solutons. You can just plug the codes into R and try it out if you
are curious.


# problem 1: Here, I am setting up a sample edge list consisting of 5
individuals with unique IDs: 8, 27, 123, 356 and 900. this will produce an
unreasonable network object because it tries to create a node for all values
between 1 and 900

Focal=c(356,123,27,8,900)
Interactor=c(123,8,900,27,356)
el=as.data.frame(cbind(Focal,Interactor))
net=network(el,matrix.type="edgelist",directed=FALSE)
summary(net)

# this yields:
Network attributes:
 vertices = 900
 directed = FALSE
 hyper = FALSE
 loops = FALSE
 multiple = FALSE
 bipartite = FALSE
 total edges = 5
   missing edges = 0
   non-missing edges = 5
 density = 1.235941e-05
... clearly not right.

## problem 2: trying to get around this by changing the IDs to characters
makes the matrix funky:
Focal=as.character(c(356,123,27,8,900))
Interactor=as.character(c(123,8,900,27,356))
el=as.data.frame(cbind(Focal,Interactor))
net=network(el,matrix.type="edgelist",directed=FALSE)
summary(net)

#This yields:
Network attributes:
 vertices = 5
 directed = FALSE
 hyper = FALSE
 loops = FALSE
 multiple = FALSE
 bipartite = FALSE
 total edges = 5
   missing edges = 0
   non-missing edges = 5
 density = 0.5


Network adjacency matrix:
    123 27 356 8 900
123   0  0   1 1   0
27    0  0   0 1   1
356   1  0   0 0   1
8     1  1   0 0   0
900   0  1   1 0   0

#So here, the network is ok, but the resulting adjacency matrix puts the ID
numbers in funky order: (123, 27, 356, 8, 900)


### solution 1: convert IDs to 3-digit string with leading 0s. This way, the
character strings will sort correctly in the adjacency matrix####
Focal=c(356,123,27,8,900)
Interactor=c(123,8,900,27,356)
el=as.data.frame(cbind(Focal,Interactor))
el$Focal=as.character(sprintf("%03d",el$Focal))
el$Interactor=as.character(sprintf("%03d",el$Interactor))
net=network(el,matrix.type="edgelist",directed=FALSE)
summary(net)

The resulting adjacency matrix:
Network adjacency matrix:
    008 027 123 356 900
008   0   1   1   0   0
027   1   0   0   0   1
123   1   0   0   1   0
356   0   0   1   0   1
900   0   1   0   1   0


### solution 2: Re-code the ID into sequential numbers, and then retrieve
the appropriate ID numbers after establishing the network object
Focal=c(356,123,27,8,900)
Interactor=c(123,8,900,27,356)
el=as.data.frame(cbind(Focal,Interactor))
code=sort(unique(c(el[,1],el[,2])))
el[,1]=match(el[,1],code)
el[,2]=match(el[,2],code)
net=network(el,matrix.type="edgelist",directed=FALSE)
network.vertex.names(net)=code
summary(net)

The resulting matrix:
Network adjacency matrix:
    8 27 123 356 900
8   0  1   1   0   0
27  1  0   0   0   1
123 1  0   0   1   0
356 0  0   1   0   1
900 0  1   0   1   0


... I learned a lot from this exercise, so I thought I'd share the
knowledge. Thanks to all those who were kind enough to reply.

Dai

> The issue here is that the edgelist->network conversion assumes that your
> data is given in the form of vertex IDs (since you are using a numeric
> matrix).  Vertex IDs are not names, but the sort order of the vertex; thus,
> you can't have an ID (in the sense of the network package) of 112998 on a
> 43-node network.  You can, of course, have a vertex that carries this number
> as a name (or other attribute).
>
> As this suggests, one approach is to renumber your edgelists prior to
> conversion.  E.g., something like this:
>
> #Let el be your edgelist matrix
> uvert<-sort(unique(c(el[,1],el[,2])))
> el[,1]<-match(el[,1],uvert)
> el[,2]<-match(el[,2],uvert)
>
> This will keep your network vertex IDs in the same order as your own ID
> numbers (names).  Then, set the vertex names (or any other attribute) equal
> to uvert; you can retrieve the original names in the usual fashion using %v%
> or get.vertex.attribute.
>
> If you don't like that road, another option is to convert your numbers to
> fixed-width character strings with leading zeros.  (formatC will do this.)
>  That ensures that the sort order matches the numeric order of your vertex
> names.  Finally, you could just create the network as usual, and then
> permute the vertices into your desired order using permute.vertexIDs (with
> the order identified by order(as.numeric(vertex.names(mynet))) or some
> such).
>
> Any of these should work, but I recommend the first, FWIW.
>
> Hope that helps,

subject ID numbers assigned from earlier analyses, which I wanted to

in the usual manner, I simply deleted those isolates like this:

and their attributes.  Incidentally, if anyone sees a flaw in my
approach, please let me know.

You can use as.matrix along with the appropriate matrix.type argument,  
as in:

 > data(g4)

    V1 V2 V3 V4
V1  0  1  1  1
V2  0  0  0  0
V3  1  0  0  0
V4  0  0  1  0
 > as.matrix(g4, "edgelist")
      [,1] [,2]
[1,]    3    1
[2,]    1    2
[3,]    1    3
[4,]    4    3
[5,]    1    4

In your example, just type
  as.matrix(y, "adjacency")

See ?as.matrix.network for details.

Dave
